avg_hr_scored.description: What the engine will actually DIVIDE BY when it scores this session: the in-band mean of its HR stream when the surviving samples span at least half the LONGER of that stream's own extent and the session's moving time, the stored `avg_hr` otherwise (#311). Publishing it here is what makes a broken reading detectable from the listing (#319). Before, `avg_hr` was echoed raw beside `hr_known: true` and an agent had to apply the 35-220 bound itself — which stopped identifying refused rows once the engine began scoring from streams, since a session can store 18 bpm and score perfectly well. The rule runs ONE WAY: `avg_hr_scored` outside 35-220 means the EF and speed/HR lenses refuse the row. The converse does NOT hold and an earlier version of this sentence claimed it did — those lenses also need a NORMALIZED-power `load_model` — `power_stream` or `weighted_watts`, not merely a non-zero `np_w`, and 32 rows publish a positive `np_w` under `avg_watts` and are refused — or distance and moving time for speed/HR, so 45 sessions on the reference database sit inside the bound and are refused by both anyway. An in-band reading is necessary, not sufficient. The one-way direction is firm for a structural reason: `avg_hr_stream` is a mean of already in-band samples, so it can never itself be out of band — this field is outside the bound only when no stream mean was available — either the stored average was used and is itself implausible (3 rows), or nothing was recorded at all and it fell to 0 (66 rows, all `hr_known: false`). Note also that a large gap between the two fields, not merely any gap, is what indicates a lossy stream: 669 of 738 rows differ at all, because Strava stores one decimal against a full-precision mean, while only 11 differ by more than 15 bpm. And `hr_known` splits the out-of-band rows into the 3 that recorded a broken reading from the 66 that recorded none, which is the difference between repairing an activity and buying a strap. `hr_known` still answers the separate question of whether a reading was recorded at all.

date_known.description: Whether `date` could be read. False means the row's stored `start_local` is NULL, empty, malformed, or dated before year 1000 — `date` is then an empty string, which is a HOLE and not a value. Needed because an empty date string already means something else in this contract: SKILL.md documents `last_hard_session_date` as `'' = none on record`, so without this flag a consumer cannot tell 'no such thing exists' from 'it exists and its date is unreadable'. #249 chose to REPORT these rows rather than refuse, because a listing cannot turn a wrong date into a wrong answer, and hoists them to the top so no limit hides them; this is the field that says which ones they are.

rankable.description: Whether the engine will give this row a ranking position. False means `start_local` is unusable as a timestamp — either its DATE half is unreadable (see `date_known`) or its TIME half is, as in `2026-08-23T37:00:00Z`, which has a perfectly readable date. These are the rows `stride activities` HOISTS to the top as needing repair, so this is the field that says why row one is row one. `rankable` means chronologically orderable: a row can be unrankable and still appear on a `top` leaderboard, carrying the same needs-repair meaning `date_known` does. It licenses no magnitude — unlike the `_known` flags, which each vouch for a value published beside them.
